quote: On the map, it just shows a tree. Is your home,
stewart_read: The rep's satellite-map observation reads as a routine verify check but lands as an implicit challenge to the customer's home, triggering a defensive reaction. This is address verification gone slightly off-script rather than an intro-legitimacy issue, since the call already used the standard online-form intro.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep could have simply asked 'is your home a single family, motor home, or manufactured home' without referencing the map at all, avoiding the friction entirely.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to drop the map commentary and go straight to the scripted home-type question; volunteering unprompted observations about the customer's property invites unnecessary pushback.

quote: Oh, well, then I don't qualify because that's under a 100.
stewart_read: The customer hands the rep a bill anchor and simultaneously voices a self-disqualifying belief. This is exactly the kind of moment where a bill-based objection should be flipped into a reason to still move forward, but the rep gives a thin denial instead.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may have judged that no flip was needed since the customer immediately said 'keep going then' and dropped the concern herself, making further reassurance unnecessary.
coaching_implication: Practice a one-line explanation for why lower bills can still qualify (e.g., tying to usage patterns or future needs) instead of a bare 'that doesn't mean you don't qualify' — the bare denial leaves the customer's underlying doubt unaddressed even though she moved on.

quote: My highest bill I'm have natural gas. My highest electric bill has been $75, and that's a bit of an anomaly.
stewart_read: The customer gives a specific, usable bill figure ($75) and even qualifies it as unusual, but the rep only replies with a flat reassurance and moves straight to the roof question — the number is filed, not flipped into urgency or curiosity.
coaching_implication: This is the clearest missed bill-anchor moment on the call; the rep should acknowledge the number specifically and connect it to what a system could do, rather than immediately pivoting to roof type.

quote: It's flat. Okay. I I wouldn't put it on the roof. I'm not putting anything on a flat roof.
stewart_read: The customer's flat roof triggers a real capability question — Ion's schema does not document flat-roof/no-ground-mount as a formal DQ rule, so this is an area where the rep is operating without documented guidance rather than following an established hard gate.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may be correctly reciting known company policy that ground-mount isn't offered, in which case this isn't a knowledge gap but accurate real-time information — the transcript alone can't confirm which.
coaching_implication: Flag for Kenny: is flat-roof-plus-no-ground-mount actually a hard DQ, or should the rep have said 'let me check with the specialist' instead of confirming disqualification unilaterally on the call? This needs to be documented in dq_rules either way.

quote: Oh, okay. Where are we going? To go outside on the ground. Oh, we don't do that.
stewart_read: The rep makes a real-time capability determination ('we don't do that') that closes out the lead entirely, rather than using the universal escape hatch to let a specialist confirm feasibility. This ends the call on the setter's unilateral judgment rather than routing an ambiguous case forward.
alternative_hypothesis: If Ion genuinely never does ground-mount installs, this is simply an accurate, efficient answer that correctly saves everyone's time rather than a scope violation.
coaching_implication: Because the schema does not confirm this is real policy, coach the rep to route flat-roof/ground-mount questions to the specialist rather than closing the lead outright — even if the answer turns out to be correct, this is the kind of edge case that should be verified rather than decided solo.

quote: Oh, okay. Well, then it won't work. Well, thanks for getting back to me. You too. Bye bye.
stewart_read: The call ends abruptly with the customer closing it out; there is no attempt from the rep to hold the door open (e.g., offering to double-check with a specialist or leaving room for a callback) before the customer says goodbye.
alternative_hypothesis: Given the immediately preceding hard 'we don't do that,' the customer's exit may have been unavoidable regardless of what the rep said next, since ground-mount was framed as flatly unavailable.
coaching_implication: Even on likely-DQ calls, the rep should have a closing line ready ('let me confirm with our team and get back to you') rather than letting the customer be the one to end the call — this preserves the lead if the flat-roof rule turns out to be more flexible than stated.

quote: and that's a bit of an anomaly. So I'm not That's good. That's why I asked you if that was just electric because then I'm under a $100 a month.
stewart_read: The customer is actively working through her own bill math out loud, essentially self-qualifying and self-disqualifying in real time — this is a moment where curiosity about her actual usage/savings potential could have been created, but the rep lets her reach her own low-bill conclusion unchallenged.
coaching_implication: Train the rep to catch when a customer is thinking out loud about qualification and step in with a curiosity-building question (e.g., about usage patterns beyond just the bill total) rather than letting her self-conclude.
